title: Notion for writers on Mac: a practical setup for drafts, research and offline work
metaTitle: Notion for writers on Mac: drafts, offline and version history
description: Notion for writers on Mac: install the desktop app, build a drafts database, check file limits and work offline. Lazur guides you through each step.
intro: Notion for writers on Mac runs best as the desktop app, with one database for every piece you write. Install the app, build a drafts table, then decide how you will handle offline work and version history. Lazur can guide you through each step out loud while you keep writing.
tldr: Use the Mac desktop app from notion.com/desktop. It updates itself, and you can check by hand from the Notion menu bar.
Build one drafts database with a Status property and a Due date. Each piece is one row, and each row is a full page.
Version history on the Free plan keeps 7 days. Plus keeps 30 days and Business keeps 90 days, so copy drafts before big rewrites.
Offline works in the Mac app, not the browser. Only the first 50 rows of a database download, and embeds and AI need a connection.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask Lazur about what is on screen. Hold fn to dictate text at the cursor in any app.

blocks.text: Install the Notion desktop app on your Mac

Notion for writers on Mac starts with the right app. Go to notion.com/desktop and click Download for macOS. Open the downloaded file and follow the prompts. The app updates itself, so you do not have to hunt for new versions.

If you want to check by hand, open Notion > Check for Updates from the menu bar. Notion's release notes cite Notion 3.8, dated Oct 13, 2026, as a recent version. Your copy may be newer by the time you read this, so check the release notes page too.
The desktop app matters for writing for one reason. It works offline, and the web version does not. You will see how that plays out in the offline section below.

Check one optional setting before you settle in. The desktop app has a Desktop beta in Settings > Preferences. It changes how tabs and windows behave. Leave it off until you know you want it. Writers who juggle several drafts in separate windows may like it. Writers who prefer one clean window may not.
Use Command Search to find drafts fast

Command Search is on by default. It lets you search your workspace or ask Notion AI from outside the Notion window. You can open it with a keyboard shortcut, from the menu bar, or from the Dock. That means you can find a half-written paragraph without opening the app first.

Think about how you search while drafting. You usually remember one phrase from the piece, not the page title. Command Search and the in-app search both work for that. For the full set of filters, read [how to search your workspace in Notion](/how-to/search-your-workspace-in-notion).

Notion also opens at login by default. For a writer who starts the day in a draft, that is handy. If you would rather open Notion when you choose, look for the login option in Settings. Check it once, so you know the setting before you need it.
Build a drafts database for every piece

One database beats a pile of loose pages. Create a database and add a Status property with the values Idea, Drafting, Editing, and Published. Add a Due date property too. Each piece becomes one row, and each row opens as a full page where you write.

Notion's Basic Content Calendar template gives you a simple start for scheduling. Open notion.com/templates/content-calendar and duplicate the template into your workspace. The template page does not list a price or a formal description, so you judge it by using it for a month.

Here is a worked example. You publish one article each week. Set the Due date to the Friday before it goes live. Set Status to Editing when the draft is done. Each Friday, you open the table and see what is late, what is in review, and what is scheduled.

To see only the work in progress, filter the view to Status is Drafting. The steps are in [how to filter a database in Notion](/how-to/filter-a-database-in-notion). Keep that filter as a second view, so you do not rebuild it each morning. A second view costs you nothing and saves a few clicks every day.
Mistakes writers make with databases
Most writers make the same few mistakes. Read this list before you build the table, so you can skip them.

items: Making a new database for each month. Use one table and a Published status instead, so the year stays in one place.
Keeping research inside the draft page. Put sources in a toggle so the draft stays readable. The steps are in [how to create a toggle in Notion](/how-to/create-a-toggle-in-notion).
Panicking when rows seem to vanish. Check the view filters first. A filter hides rows without deleting them, and clearing it brings them back.
Skipping the template. A template keeps every new piece the same shape. Learn it with [how to create a template in Notion](/how-to/create-a-template-in-notion).

blocks.text: Filters cause most of the lost-row panic. When a row disappears, open the filter bar before you search the trash. That order saves time. Most missing rows are sitting behind a filter you set last week.
Attachments, sources and file size limits
Writers attach a lot. PDFs, interview audio, screenshots, and scanned notes all count. Know the limit before you drop a big file into a draft.

On the Free plan, each file can be up to 5 MB. On Plus, Business, and Enterprise, each file can be up to 5 GB. That gap matters for audio. A long interview recording can pass 5 MB easily, so check the file size before you upload it.

Keep heavy files where they belong. Store large recordings in your own cloud folder, then paste a link into the draft. Put that link in a sources toggle, so an editor can follow the trail back to the material. The link does the work the file used to do.

A source list works best in a simple format. Write the author, the title, the date, and the link on one line. If a source is a PDF on your screen, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to explain a section. Lazur answers out loud. It does not edit the PDF for you.
Version history on Free, Plus and Business

Version history is your safety net for weeks of edits. It is not a permanent archive. On Free, Notion keeps version history for 7 days. Plus keeps 30 days. Business keeps 90 days. Enterprise uses a custom period set by the contract.

That changes how you should work. Say you rewrite a chapter every month on Free. The version you want may be gone by the time you look for it. Before a big rewrite, duplicate the page. The copy becomes your fixed snapshot. Put the date in its title, so you can find it later.

Deleted pages follow a different path. Check Trash before you assume a draft is gone. The steps are in [how to restore a deleted page in Notion](/how-to/restore-a-deleted-page-in-notion). Restoring from Trash is faster than rebuilding from memory.
Pricing decides which history you get. Free costs $0. Plus costs $10 per member per month. Business costs $20 per member per month. Check notion.com/pricing before you buy, since prices can change.
Which Notion plan fits a solo writer

A solo writer can often stay on Free. The pricing page says a solo workspace can add as many blocks as you like. The block limit on Free applies to workspaces with more than one member. So you will not hit a block cap on your own.

Look at the file size and version history instead. Those two limits matter more to a writer working alone. If you need 30 days of history, or files larger than 5 MB, compare Plus against your current plan. Then pick the cheapest option that covers both.

A writer who shares drafts with an editor should compare plans with the editor in mind. Business is the plan with 90 days of version history. Check the pricing page for the current team terms before you decide.
Writing offline on a Mac with no connection
Offline mode is where the desktop app earns its place. Offline pages work in the Mac and mobile apps, not in a web browser. Every workspace member can use offline pages on every plan.

On paid plans, Notion downloads recently visited and favorited pages for you. You can turn that off under Settings > Offline. If you travel often, leave it on. Then the pages you opened last week are on your Mac when the Wi-Fi drops.

Databases have one catch. Only the first 50 rows of the first view download for offline use. Make your offline view small. Filter it to the drafts you are working on, and set that view as the first one in the database.

Some things still need a connection. Embeds from other apps, AI blocks, forms, and buttons need the internet. You also cannot share a page or change its permissions offline. Share the page before you get on the plane, not after.

items: Open the drafts database and set the first view to Status is Drafting.
Open each active draft once, so it counts as recently visited.
Turn off Wi-Fi and confirm each draft still opens and scrolls.
Share pages and change permissions before you leave.

blocks.text: Where Lazur fits in a writing session

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It works in any app, so you can ask about the Notion page you have open. It is not a plugin or add-in for Notion or any other app.

Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. This helps when a menu shifts between app versions. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click, so you stay in control of the mouse.

A typical session looks like this. You have a drafts table open in Notion. You hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask why a row is missing. Lazur reads the filter bar on screen and says which filter hides it. You clear that filter, then go back to writing.
Dictate first drafts with fn

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. The words land where your cursor sits, so you can dictate straight into a Notion page. Dictation is included and is not the headline feature. Many writers still find it the fastest way to get a messy first draft down.

Dictation works best with a plan. Outline the sections as headings first. Then talk one section at a time. Snippets store text you reuse, such as a standard byline or a sign-off. Clipboard slots keep a few copied passages ready while you write.

To see your own speed, run the [typing speed test](/tools/typing-speed-test) and the [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test). Compare the two results. Then decide where dictation fits in your routine, and where typing still wins.
Privacy and what leaves your Mac
Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, and that memory stays on your Mac. That helps when you ask a follow-up later in the week. Notion has its own data terms. Read them on Notion's site before you put client material in a shared workspace.
Next steps for your Notion writing setup

items: Download the desktop app from notion.com/desktop and try Command Search once.
Duplicate the Basic Content Calendar template and rename it for your drafts.
Add a Status property and set up the Drafting and Editing values.
Check your largest attachment against the 5 MB limit on Free.
Make an offline view of the first 50 rows and test it with Wi-Fi off.

blocks.text: Start small. A drafts database with four statuses is enough for most solo writers. Add structure only when a real problem shows up, and fix that problem first.

faq.question: Is Notion for writers on Mac better in the app or the browser?
faq.answer: The desktop app is the better choice for most writers on a Mac. Offline pages work in the Mac and mobile apps, but not in a web browser. The app also updates itself, so you do not have to track new versions by hand.

faq.question: How do I check for a new Notion version on Mac?
faq.answer: Open Notion > Check for Updates from the menu bar. Notion updates the app automatically, so a manual check is only for when you want to confirm. Notion's release notes cite Notion 3.8, dated Oct 13, 2026, as a recent version.

faq.question: What is the largest file I can attach to a Notion page on the Free plan?
faq.answer: The Free plan allows up to 5 MB per file. Plus, Business, and Enterprise allow up to 5 GB per file. For interview audio or long scans, check the file size first, or store the file elsewhere and link to it.

faq.question: How long does Notion keep version history for writers?
faq.answer: Free keeps version history for 7 days. Plus keeps 30 days, and Business keeps 90 days. Enterprise uses a custom period. Duplicate a page before a big rewrite if you are on Free, so you keep a fixed copy.

faq.question: Can I write in Notion offline on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes, in the Mac app, if the pages were downloaded first. Only the first 50 rows of the first database view download. Embeds, AI blocks, forms, and buttons need a connection. You cannot share a page or change its permissions offline.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Notion?
faq.answer: Lazur works in any app, including Notion. It sees your screen only while you hold the shortcut, and it answers out loud. Lazur does not click buttons or operate Notion for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for Notion or any other app.

faq.question: How much does Notion cost for a solo writer?
faq.answer: Free costs $0. Plus costs $10 per member per month, and Business costs $20 per member per month. Check the pricing page at notion.com/pricing before you buy, since plans and prices can change.

faq.question: Can Lazur help me dictate a first draft into Notion?
faq.answer: Yes. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, including a Notion page. Lazur also supports snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots. Test your speed with the typing speed test before you rely on it.
